newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Canada sees need to tackle new pollution.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Canada sees need to tackle new pollution.

text.p: The United States and Canada need to work harder to tackle smog and other lung-clogging particles blowing across the border, the two governments said in a report released on Friday.
In the first five-year review of a 1991 air quality agreement, however, the two countries concluded they had met their goals for curbing sulfur dioxide emissions, which create acid rain.
"The Parties agreed ... that control of transboundary air pollution has not occurred to the extent necessary to fully protect the environment," the report said.

While the air quality pact focused on acid rain, which was the biggest cross-border problem for many years, "ground-level ozone, air toxics, and inhalable particles are becoming increasingly important areas of concern," it said.
The two governments said they had begun to study regional smog controls and would look at managing air toxics, such as mercury, benzene and dioxins.

Sulfur dioxide emissions in the United States were down in 1995 by more than 50 percent or almost 5 million tons from 1980 levels, largely thanks to emissions cuts at coal-burning power plants, according to the report.
In eastern Canada, sulfur dioxide emissions in 1994 were also slashed by more than half to 1.7 million tons from 1980, exceeding goals for the region.
The report said the two countries were also on their way to meeting 10 percent cuts in nitrogen oxide pollution by 2000.
